title: The Supply Side of Social Media
abstract: We study an overlooked feature of social media platforms: their distinctive model of content production. Unlike legacy media outlets, platforms do not professionally produce content ex-ante optimized to appeal to viewers; instead, they rely on large numbers of amateur users creating content in pursuit of social status, expressive satisfaction, or creative fulfilment. The resulting scale of their content libraries allows them to ex-post cherry-pick the pieces most appealing to viewers. We develop an equilibrium model of this process. We show that because the scale powering platforms' cherry-picking concentrates where creators are eager to produce, creators' supply-side preferences can influence what viewers consume. Collecting new data on Instagram, TikTok, and X/Twitter, we show that most of the content in viewers' feeds is created by non-professionals who tend to produce envy-provoking “lifestyle” and partisan political content. To separate supply- and demand-side preferences, we experimentally manipulate viewers' feeds and pay creators to post different types of content. Piece-by-piece, lifestyle and partisan political content is less likely to highly engage viewers than more benign entertainment. But the social status and expressive satisfaction creators derive from creating such content lead it to be produced at such a large scale that platforms can cherry-pick the minority of pieces viewers find more interesting or entertaining than the marginal piece of entertainment. Estimating our model using the experimental variation, we calculate that supply-side preferences account for one-third to one-half of the prevalence of lifestyle and partisan content in viewers' feeds.
